title: The Surveillance Classroom
author: Walled Garden
summary: The Walled Garden essay examines the deployment of AI-enabled emotional surveillance technologies in schools -- systems that monitor students' disposition, affect, and concentration during screen-based work. The author frames surveillance technologies as pedagogical acts: every design choice a school makes about which tools to use teaches students something about what the institution believes about them. Drawing on Emerson's trust principle and research on surveillance effects, the piece argues that surveillance produces the opposite of what trust produces. When people feel watched, they experience increased stress and anxiety, pressure to perform rather than learn, and explicit erosion of institutional trust. The essay connects surveillance technologies to broader trends in school design, arguing that the decision to surveil is also a decision about what kind of relationship the school wants with its students.
points: * School technology choices are pedagogical acts: what gets monitored, measured, and recorded teaches students what their school believes about who they are. * AI-enabled emotional surveillance monitors disposition, affect, and concentration -- not just keystrokes and time-on-task -- representing a qualitative intensification of behavioral monitoring. * Research consistently shows that people under surveillance experience heightened stress, performance pressure, and explicitly reduced trust in those surveilling them. * The surveillance classroom teaches a specific lesson: learning is compliance under observation, not genuine inquiry in a trusting environment. * Emerson's principle -- 'trust men and they will be true to you; treat them greatly and they will show themselves great' -- names the opposite of what surveillance achieves.
quotes: Which tools they use, which metrics they record, and which software they license are all pedagogical acts.
This piece asks what surveillance technologies teach students about what their schools believe about them.
Trust and Its Enemies "Trust men and they will be true to you; treat them greatly and they will show themselves great." Ralph Waldo Emerson wrote those words in 1841.

Nearly two centuries later, trust remains an essential element of any healthy community, which is why I was concerned to read about the rise of AI-enabled "emotional surveillance" technologies in The Atlantic .
These products monitor people's disposition, affect, and concentration during screen-based work.
They can tell you if someone appears interested or impatient, agreeable or skeptical.
They surveil to produce insights about performance and productivity.
